title: Can you run batch jobs in Vert.x (setPeriodic, worker verticles/executeBlocking, Quartz cron)?
shortTitle: Can you run batch jobs in Vert.x (setPeriodic, worker verticles/executeBlocking, Quartz cron)?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. Vert.x supports batch and scheduled work through several mechanisms. `vertx.setPeriodic(interval, handler)` and `vertx.setTimer(delay, handler)` fire callbacks on the event loop at fixed intervals or after a delay for lightweight scheduling. Because the actual batch processing is usually CPU- or I/O-heavy and would violate the non-blocking rule, you run it on worker threads via `executeBlocking` or inside a worker verticle. For calendar-style cron scheduling (for example "every weekday at 2 AM"), you integrate the Vert.x Quartz scheduler extension or a cron-parsing scheduler that computes the next fire time and arms a timer. The scheduling trigger stays on the event loop, and the heavy job runs on a worker pool.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must run an end-of-day interest posting job. The fast front-desk clerk (event loop) is not the one who should sit crunching thousands of accounts — that would freeze the counter. Instead, the clerk keeps a timer on his desk (`setPeriodic`) that rings every interval, and when it rings he hands the heavy ledger work to the back-office team (worker verticle) so the counter keeps serving customers. For jobs that must run at a specific wall-clock time like 2 AM on business days, the bank uses a proper calendar scheduler (Quartz cron) that wakes the back office at exactly the right moment.
s1_definition.oneliner: Schedule the trigger on the event loop with setPeriodic/timer or a Quartz cron, but always run the heavy batch work on a worker verticle or executeBlocking.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. Vert.x supports batch and scheduled work through several mechanisms. `vertx.setPeriodic(interval, handler)` and `vertx.setTimer(delay, handler)` fire callbacks on the event loop at fixed intervals or after a delay for lightweight scheduling. Because the actual batch processing is usually CPU- or I/O-heavy and would violate the non-blocking rule, you run it on worker threads via `executeBlocking` or inside a worker verticle. For calendar-style cron scheduling (for example "every weekday at 2 AM"), you integrate the Vert.x Quartz scheduler extension or a cron-parsing scheduler that computes the next fire time and arms a timer. The scheduling trigger stays on the event loop, and the heavy job runs on a worker pool.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must run an end-of-day interest posting job. The fast front-desk clerk (event loop) is not the one who should sit crunching thousands of accounts — that would freeze the counter. Instead, the clerk keeps a timer on his desk (`setPeriodic`) that rings every interval, and when it rings he hands the heavy ledger work to the back-office team (worker verticle) so the counter keeps serving customers. For jobs that must run at a specific wall-clock time like 2 AM on business days, the bank uses a proper calendar scheduler (Quartz cron) that wakes the back office at exactly the right moment.

**One line to remember:** Schedule the trigger on the event loop with setPeriodic/timer or a Quartz cron, but always run the heavy batch work on a worker verticle or executeBlocking.

sections.s2_technical:
For simple fixed-rate scheduling, `vertx.setPeriodic(60000, id -> runJob())` fires every 60 seconds and returns a timer id you can cancel with `vertx.cancelTimer(id)`. `vertx.setTimer(5000, id -> runOnce())` fires once after a delay. These handlers execute on the event loop, so the handler itself must not block; its job is only to kick off the real work. For example a reconciliation trigger might simply call a method that submits the heavy work to a worker.

The heavy work must leave the event loop. The two standard ways are `executeBlocking`, which runs a blocking lambda on the worker pool and returns a Future, and worker verticles, which are deployed with `new DeploymentOptions().setWorker(true)` and run entirely on worker threads so their handlers may block. For a large batch you typically deploy a worker verticle and trigger it over the event bus, or call `vertx.executeBlocking(promise -> { processAllAccounts(); promise.complete(); }, false)` where the `false` means do not require ordered execution so multiple batches can run in parallel. You can also use `WorkerExecutor` created by `vertx.createSharedWorkerExecutor("batch-pool", 10)` to get a dedicated, sized pool for batch work so it does not starve ordinary worker tasks.

For calendar/cron scheduling, `setPeriodic` is not enough because it only does fixed intervals, not "2 AM on weekdays." The common solution is the Vert.x Quartz extension or a cron library: you parse a cron expression, compute the delay until the next fire time, and arm `setTimer` for that delay; when it fires you run the job on a worker and re-arm for the following occurrence. Senior nuances matter here. First, in a clustered deployment you must prevent every node from running the same cron job simultaneously, so you add leader election or a distributed lock (for example a shared map lock on the cluster manager, or a database advisory lock) so only one node executes. Second, long batch jobs should report progress and be idempotent and restartable, because a node can crash mid-batch. Third, you should size the worker pool deliberately and monitor event-loop lag, because a flood of batch tasks can still exhaust workers and delay triggers. Fourth, for very large data sets prefer streaming and chunking (process in pages, commit per chunk) over loading everything into memory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must post daily interest to every savings account at a scheduled time without freezing its live APIs. If the interest calculation ran on the event loop it would stall thousands of customer requests. This is exactly why the trigger uses a timer but the calculation runs on a worker — the event loop only kicks off the job.

Problem 2 — The interest run touches many accounts and is I/O-heavy, so it must run on a dedicated pool and be resilient. This is exactly what a sized `WorkerExecutor` plus `executeBlocking` gives — isolated worker threads that may block safely.

Problem 3 — The business wants the job at a specific time, modeled here with a periodic trigger that represents the daily cron, and in production a Quartz cron plus a cluster lock so only one node runs it. This is exactly how cron scheduling plus leader election works.

The demo schedules an interest-posting batch with `setPeriodic` (standing in for a daily cron), runs the heavy posting on a dedicated worker executor, and processes Rajesh's and Priya's accounts idempotently. Classes and steps: `BatchVerticle` (schedules the trigger, owns the worker executor), `InterestBatchJob` (the blocking job that posts interest), `Account` (domain), and `BankApp` (main).

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run (prints a batch run every 5 seconds)
java -jar target/vertx-interest-batch-1.0.0-fat.jar
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1,000,000) and Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250,000); daily interest at a 4% annual rate.

Step 1 — `BatchVerticle` arms `setPeriodic` (standing in for the 2 AM cron). The timer handler runs on the event loop and fires every interval.

Step 2 — When the timer fires, the handler does not do heavy work itself. It submits the job to the dedicated `interest-batch-pool` via `executeBlocking`, so the event loop immediately returns to serving other events.

Step 3 — On a worker thread, `InterestBatchJob.postDailyInterest` iterates the accounts. For Rajesh it computes 1,000,000 times the daily rate, rounds to two decimals, credits his balance, and logs it. It does the same for Priya. The per-account blocking write is safe because it is off the event loop.

Step 4 — The job returns the total interest posted, which flows back as a Future result, and the `onSuccess` callback on the event loop logs the batch completion. The job is idempotent and chunked so a crash can be retried safely.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Interest batch scheduled.
2026-10-26 14:55:16 [INFO] Cron trigger fired (timer=0) — submitting batch to worker pool
2026-10-26 14:55:16 [INFO] Interest posted: SAV2001 += Rs.109.59
2026-10-26 14:55:16 [INFO] Interest posted: CUR3001 += Rs.27.40
2026-10-26 14:55:16 [INFO] Batch complete. Total interest posted: Rs.136.99
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  setPeriodic(5000)  [EVENT LOOP]
    │ timer fires
    ▼
  handler (EVENT LOOP — does NOT block)
    │ batchPool.executeBlocking(...)   ← submit to worker pool
    │ (event loop returns immediately)
    ▼
  interest-batch-pool (WORKER threads, size 4)
    │ InterestBatchJob.postDailyInterest(accounts)
    │   SAV2001: 1,000,000 × dailyRate = +Rs.109.59
    │   CUR3001:   250,000 × dailyRate = +Rs.27.40
    │ return total Rs.136.99
    ▼
  onSuccess (EVENT LOOP)  ───→ log "Batch complete Rs.136.99"

  Production cron: parse "0 0 2 * * ?" → setTimer(next 02:00) → run → re-arm
                   + cluster lock so ONLY the leader node runs it
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, Vert.x runs batch and scheduled jobs well, as long as you respect the golden rule of never blocking the event loop. For simple fixed-rate scheduling I use setPeriodic, which fires a handler on the event loop at an interval and returns a timer id I can cancel, or setTimer for a one-shot delay. The crucial discipline is that the timer handler itself does almost nothing; its only job is to kick off the real work somewhere safe. The heavy batch processing goes onto worker threads, either through executeBlocking, which runs a blocking lambda on the worker pool and returns a future, or inside a dedicated worker verticle, and for isolation I create a sized shared worker executor so batch work never starves ordinary tasks.

For calendar-style cron scheduling, setPeriodic alone is not enough because it only does fixed intervals, not something like 2 AM on business days. There I use the Vert.x Quartz extension or a cron parser: I compute the delay until the next fire time, arm a timer for that delay, run the job on a worker, and re-arm for the following occurrence.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I built exactly this for daily interest posting. A batch verticle schedules the trigger, and when it fires it submits the interest job to a dedicated worker pool via executeBlocking, so the event loop stays free to serve live balance and transfer requests. The job walks each account, computes the daily interest on the balance using BigDecimal, credits Rajesh and Priya, and returns the total, and it is written to be idempotent and chunked so it can be retried safely after a crash. In production I run it on a cron schedule and, because we run a Vert.x cluster, I guard it with a distributed lock so only the leader node executes the run and we never double-post interest.

So in an interview I answer it as: schedule the trigger on the event loop with setPeriodic, a timer, or a Quartz cron, but always push the actual batch work onto a worker verticle or executeBlocking, size the worker pool deliberately, and in a cluster add leader election so the job runs exactly once.
